transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-16
Start: 08:43 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Torres (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Lopez (CTO - Atlantic Warehousing), Sana Malik (Head of Engineering), Ethan Wu (Infra Lead)

Summary: quick discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and the tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer wants multi-region failover, deterministic SLAs for transactional API calls, and clarity on automatic fallback behavior when a region or model is degraded.

Topics: multi-region routing, fallback policies, SLA expectations, model variant fallbacks, KV cache and prefix cache behavior, network isolation for Private, testing plan for POC.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Alex: All right good morning everyone, thanks for joining. uh i'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya on the SE side. how are you all?
[00:08] Mark: Morning alex, doing well. we have a tight agenda — high level reliability requirements and how you handle incidents and fallbacks.
[00:14] Sana: hi alex, thanks. we want to understand if we go Hosted today, what happens when a region blips, and how predictable the latency/SLA is for our transactional use case.
[00:23] Alex: totally — that's what we're here for. quick question, what's your current setup? are you calling multiple providers today?
[00:28] Ethan: we have internal microservices in GCP us-east and us-west, and for ML we currently call VendorX endpoints in us-east only. looking to move to a single platform with multi-region.
[00:39] Priya: okay got it. a couple of things we usually look at: routing policies (latency-priority vs cost-priority), automatic fallback to compatible model variants, and multi-region active-passive or active-active options. for Hosted, we can route by region with automatic fallback to another region or to a cheaper model if capacity constrained.
[00:54] Mark: how does that fallback work in practice? is there a connection-level retry? does state like KV/cache survive when you cross regions?
[01:03] Priya: good q. so for prefix / KV cache — that is node-local, and in Hosted it's region-local by default. if you failover to another region you won't have the same warm KV cache, so cold starts will be heavier. we do however have optional cross-region cache warmup strategies in Dedicated and Private where you can pre-populate or replicate hot keys.
[01:27] Sana: replication sounds interesting. does that add latency or cost?
[01:31] Priya: there's an overhead — replication adds write amplification and some network egress. it's a config knob in Dedicated/Private, less commonly enabled for hosted unless you need strict session affinity.
[01:43] Ethan: SLA expectations — what do you guarantee for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?
[01:47] Alex: Hosted has an SLA for uptime and a measured p99 latency target for our verified configs; Dedicated offers stronger, contract-backed SLAs with reserved pools, and Private is customer-controlled so we provide platform uptime for the control plane but the infra SLA is customer-managed in on-prem cases. i can send the exact SLA table.
[02:03] Mark: please do. for our transactional API calls, we need sub-300ms p95 in steady state, and an availability target of 99.95 regionally. is that realistic with Hosted?
[02:13] Priya: sub-300ms p95 depends on model and prompt length; for smaller models and optimized kernels we see that in single-region hosted configs — but consistent SLA commitments are usually within Dedicated where we reserve capacity and can tune batching and kernels for your seq len distribution.
[02:30] Mark: ok so Dedicated for strict latency. what about multi-region active-active? we want failover within 30s and minimal impact to customer requests.
[02:38] Priya: we support active-active with regional routing and health checks. Latency-wise, when a region fails we can fail requests over and replay them to the failover region. the main user-visible impact is the cold KV cache and potential model-variant mismatch. to limit impact we recommend a fallback policy: primary model in primary region, fallback to a slightly smaller but compatible model in failover region, with token-limited responses to reduce cost while preserving correctness.
[03:01] Sana: is the fallback automatic or something we control via policy? we want to control which model families are allowed as fallback.
[03:08] Priya: policy-driven. you can define model families, allowed quantization levels, and an ordered fallback list per route. we also log the fallback event and expose it in the Console with trace IDs so you can tie regressions to specific failovers.
[03:22] Ethan: about tracing: do you provide request-level tracing or is it just per-route metrics?
[03:26] Alex: both. the Console has per-request traces with token-level breakdowns, and you can pipe logs to your SIEM. for Dedicated and Private we can enable longer retention and more granular tracing.
[03:35] Mark: what about throttling and quotas during an incident — say a region is degraded and traffic is re-routed, do you enforce admission control?
[03:42] Priya: yes we have admission control and smart routing — you can configure burst capacity and queue length. during overflow we can automatically reduce max tokens or shard traffic to cheaper variants. the idea is graceful degradation, not hard failures.
[03:54] Sana: can we set SLAs on throughput per route? e.g., maintain 500 rps to a critical endpoint?
[04:00] Alex: yes with Dedicated we can size committed capacity to hit throughput targets, plus we have autoscaling policies for short bursts that can be tuned. for Hosted, we give throughput guidance but peak guarantees are part of dedicated contracts.
[04:12] Ethan: we are concerned about security during failover — if we route to a different region, how is data residency handled? could requests touch non-allowed regions?
[04:21] Priya: region policies are strict. you can whitelist allowed regions per customer or per route. cross-region failover only happens to whitelisted regions; if no whitelisted region is available the request will either queue or fail based on your policy. for Private deployments you keep everything in your VPC so no cross-region egress to Redwood-hosted regions occurs.
[04:45] Mark: good. about incident response: if a region has a partial outage, what is your typical detection and failover timeline?
[04:52] Alex: automated health checks detect degradation in seconds, failover orchestration typically completes within tens of seconds for the routing switch, but warm-cold effects can add a couple minutes for caches to warm. we can run canaries as part of the failover to validate.
[05:08] Sana: is there a manual override? our SREs want a kill switch to force route traffic to Private or to an alternative provider.
[05:14] Priya: yes, Console has manual routing controls; we can also integrate with your incident management (pagerduty webhook) to trigger runbooks.
[05:22] Mark: what's the behavior for in-flight requests during failover — do you retry automatically and dedupe?
[05:27] Priya: we generally retry idempotently where possible and expose dedupe tokens. we also surface trace IDs so you can reconcile. retries are configurable; for transactional operations we recommend idempotency keys.
[05:39] Ethan: we don't want unexpected model regressions during a failover — how do you handle model quality checks when falling back?
[05:46] Priya: good point. we have a model compatibility matrix and quality gates — you can attach eval sets to routes and we will block fallbacks that fail critical thresholds. non-blocking fallbacks are allowed with flagged logs.
[06:00] Alex: to add, Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload so fallbacks are less likely to cause semantic drift.
[06:08] Mark: for POC scope, we'd like a synthetic run with region failover, a soak test at 500 rps, and a correctness check on a prompt set — can Redwood run that?
[06:16] Priya: yes we can. typical POC is 2 weeks: baseline latency/throughput, then a controlled region failover and smoke checks on correctness. i'll draft a runbook.
[06:26] Sana: pricing question — if we use cross-region replication for KV cache in Dedicated, how is that priced?
[06:32] Alex: it's billed as an add-on: replication bandwidth and additional reserved capacity. i'll include a cost example in the pricing doc we send.
[06:39] Mark: do you support private control plane where the control plane runs in our VPC?
[06:43] Priya: yes that's Redwood Private — control plane endpoints inside your VPC, optional on-prem runtime. in that model you manage the infra SLA, but we provide the platform and orchestration.
[06:53] Ethan: network topology — if we go Private across two data centers, can we still use Redwood Console hosted for observability?
[06:59] Alex: yes you can opt for a hybrid model: control plane in your VPC, telemetry shipped to Redwood Console or your own observability stack. telemetry route is configurable for compliance.
[07:09] Sana: any limitations on model families in Private?
[07:12] Priya: generally no — you can bring open models and we support the same kernel optimizations. a few experimental kernels require specific GPU stacks, which we can advise on.
[07:22] Mark: how about testing upgrades and rollouts? we need canary deploys and immediate rollback on regressions.
[07:28] Priya: we support canary and A/B rollouts, automatic rollback policies based on error rates or eval regressions and manual approval gates.
[07:36] Alex: quick note about telemetry: fallback events are logged with reason codes (region-failure, capacity, manual-route) so you can see why a fallback happened.
[07:45] Ethan: do you have examples of customers who've done multi-region failover? any war stories?
[07:49] Priya: yes — we worked with a payments company (anonymized) that needed sub-250ms p95; when a US region flapped we failed over to a secondary region and used a smaller quantized variant for a transitional window; the main issue was cold cache causing a short spike in latency, which was mitigated by pre-warming hot keys.
[08:10] Mark: ok, operationally we need to understand the observability surface — what exact logs/metrics will we get?
[08:15] Alex: you'll get per-request latency, token counts, model version, fallback reason, region, and trace id. plus aggregated dashboards and export to your prometheus/grafana or s3.
[08:25] Sana: moving to timeline — we're looking to decide vendor in 6 weeks and run a pilot in May. is that feasible?
[08:31] Alex: yes that's feasible. next steps: we'll send security docs and pricing, Priya will share a POC runbook, and we'll schedule the technical deep-dive next week.
[08:40] Mark: perfect. thank you both.
[08:42] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.

End notes: minor transcription artifacts present (company names sometimes spaced, occasional mis-heard acronyms like K V cache). references to shared artifacts: "POC runbook (link)" and "SLA table (link)" were mentioned and will be attached in follow-up email.
